sentences.text: Lourinhanosaurus was a moderately large carnivorous theropod dinosaur.
The discovered specimen was a subadult measuring about 4.5 meters in length and weighing around 160 kilograms.
Lourinhanosaurus is estimated to have been 4 to 6 meters in length.
It was the first theropod dinosaur for which gastroliths — small stones swallowed to aid digestion — were definitively assigned to the animal.
Around 100 eggs, some containing embryonic bones and skin, were found in 1993 at the beach of Paimogo.
The first remains of Lourinhanosaurus were found in 1982 near Lourinhã, Portugal, but the genus was not described until 1998 by Octávio Mateus.
The only known species, L. antunesi, was named in honor of paleontologist Miguel Telles Antunes.
The most complete known specimen is the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — ML 370, a partial skeleton.

This partial skeleton includes six cervical vertebrae with ribs, five sacral vertebrae with ribs, 14 caudal vertebrae, eight chevrons, both femurs, the right tibia and fibula, one metatarsus, both ilia, pubes, ischia, and 32 associated gastroliths.
Fossil evidence suggests Lourinhanosaurus formed nesting colonies on a floodplain.
Researchers estimate that at least six females laid eggs simultaneously in an area of only 32 square meters.
There is no evidence that Lourinhanosaurus excavated nests or buried eggs; they likely laid them directly on the ground in a sunny spot near a pond.
It is probable that Lourinhanosaurus did not actively incubate its eggs.
There is no firm scientific consensus on the classification of Lourinhanosaurus.
Lourinhanosaurus was initially considered a primitive member of Allosauroidea and later discussed as closely related to Sinraptoridae.
Lourinhanosaurus is tentatively placed within the superfamily Allosauroidea.
Lourinhanosaurus lived approximately 150 to 145 million years ago during the Kimmeridgian and Tithonian stages.
Lourinhanosaurus lived from 152.21 to 145.06 million years ago.
Some researchers suggest Lourinhanosaurus may not be an allosauroid but rather a member of the more basal group Megalosauroidea.
A 2012 study by Carrano et al. classified Lourinhanosaurus as a coelurosaur.
A 2022 study refers to Lourinhanosaurus as a putative metriacanthosaurid.
